key_concept: Photocurrent is proportional to the intensity (power) of the incident light, while the stopping potential depends only on the frequency of light and the work function: $e|V_0| = h\nu - \phi$.
steps: The source power falls linearly with time, $P(t) = P_0 - kt$, but its frequency $\nu$ does not change.
Number of photons per second $= \dfrac{P}{h\nu}$. Each absorbed photon can eject at most one electron, so the number of photoelectrons per second is proportional to $P$.
Hence the saturation photocurrent $I \propto P(t)$. It decreases linearly with time and reaches zero when $P = 0$.
By Einstein's equation, $K_{max} = h\nu - \phi = e|V_0|$. This depends only on $\nu$ and $\phi$, not on intensity.
Since $\nu$ is unchanged, $|V_0|$ stays constant (a horizontal line) for as long as photoemission occurs.
Option (1) matches: $I$ falls linearly and $|V|$ is constant.
final_answer: Option (1): I vs t: straight line decreasing linearly from a positive value to zero; |V| vs t: horizontal line (constant)
why_not_others: Options (2) and (3) wrongly make the stopping potential depend on intensity. Options (3) and (4) wrongly keep the photocurrent constant even though fewer photons arrive each second.
common_trap: Thinking that lower light power means less energetic photoelectrons, and so a smaller stopping potential. In fact power changes only the number of photons, not the energy $h\nu$ of each photon.
time_saving_tip: Remember the pairing: intensity controls current, frequency controls stopping potential. Here only intensity changes, so $I$ varies and $V$ is constant.
